Maccabees
MAK-uh-beez
proper noun
The Jewish family that led the revolt against Antiochus IV (167–160 B.C.); from Maccabee, “the hammer,” the byname of Judas, son of Mattathias.

Biblical Definition

The Maccabees were the priestly family—Mattathias and his sons, chief among them Judas called Maccabeus, “the hammer”—who led the Jewish revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes in the second century before Christ, when he sought to stamp out the worship of the LORD, defiled the temple, and forbade the law on pain of death. By their resistance the temple was retaken and cleansed and the daily sacrifice restored, an event commemorated in the Feast of Dedication, which the Lord Jesus Himself observed at Jerusalem in winter. This period falls in the four hundred silent years between Malachi and the coming of Christ; the prophet Daniel had foretold the tyrant who would pollute the sanctuary and take away the daily sacrifice and set up the abomination of desolation, and the epistle to the Hebrews remembers the faithful of that age who were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Yet the dictionary marks plainly that the books of First and Second Maccabees, which record this history, are part of the Apocrypha and are not Scripture. The Protestant canon is the sixty-six inspired books; the Apocrypha, however useful for history, was never received by the Jews as canonical, is nowhere cited as Scripture by Christ or the apostles, and was given canonical standing only by Rome at the Council of Trent. The dictionary honors the Maccabean courage and the history while holding the closed Protestant canon against the Apocrypha.

Webster 1828 Definition

The priestly family who revolted against Antiochus IV, cleansed the temple, and restored the sacrifice; their history is in the Apocrypha—honored as record, not received as Scripture.

MACCABEES, the family of Mattathias and Judas “the hammer,” who revolted against Antiochus IV.

Resisted the tyrant who defiled the temple and forbade the law.

Retook and cleansed the temple, restoring the daily sacrifice.

Modern Corruption

Rome canonized the books of Maccabees and the rest of the Apocrypha at Trent; the dictionary honors the Maccabean history while holding the sixty-six-book Protestant canon.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to name is the canon. The books of First and Second Maccabees record a real and stirring history, but they are part of the Apocrypha, not the inspired Scripture. The Jews never received these books into their canon; the Lord Jesus and the apostles, who quote the Old Testament constantly, never cite them as Scripture; and the early church largely distinguished them from the canonical books. It was the Council of Trent in 1546, in reaction to the Reformation, that first dogmatically pronounced the Apocrypha canonical—in part because Second Maccabees was used to defend prayers for the dead and purgatory. The Protestant churches held the line: the canon is sixty-six books.

The principle to recover is the closed and sufficient canon. All Scripture is given by inspiration of God; the church does not add to the inspired books, however edifying a history may be. The Maccabean courage may be honored, and the Feast of Dedication the Lord kept may be remembered, and Daniel’s prophecy of the temple’s defilement read with profit; but doctrine is built on Scripture alone, and the Apocrypha, useful for history, is no part of the rule of faith. The Reformers’ verdict stands against Trent.
